title: Architecture Models
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain defense in depth, zero trust, secure-by-design, and shared responsibility, and pick the model a scenario is describing.

blocks.text: Defense in depth stacks multiple controls so a failure of one layer leaves others standing: perimeter firewall, segment gateways, host firewall, application checks, encryption, and backups. The exam phrase to expect: no single control is trusted to catch everything.

Zero trust removes the idea of a trusted internal network. Every request is authenticated, authorized, and encrypted, regardless of origin. Three core principles: verify explicitly (strong identity, device health), use least-privilege access (just enough, just in time), and assume breach (segment, encrypt, monitor inside).

items: Microsegmentation: cutting the inside network into small zones, so one compromised host reaches little.
Implicit deny: access is refused unless a rule grants it.
Continuous verification: sessions re-checked, with device posture in the decision.
Identity becomes the new perimeter: who and what asks matters more than where they sit.

blocks.text: Secure-by-design builds security into requirements from day one: threat modeling, least privilege defaults, fail-safe defaults, and keeping security simple enough to verify. It contrasts with bolting controls on after delivery. Shared responsibility draws the line between what a provider secures and what the customer secures; in the cloud the customer always keeps responsibility for data classification, identity, and access choices.

rows: Security in requirements, end to end
Provider and customer each own parts

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: Zero-trust scenarios mention device health checks, per-request authorization, or microsegmentation. Segmentation questions focus on limiting blast radius. When a question says a design assumed the internal network was safe, the fix is zero trust thinking.

blocks.title: Redesign an office network on paper
steps: Start with a flat network: one subnet holding HR laptops, a file server, and a printer, all able to reach each other.
Draw segmentation that separates those three groups with a gateway.
Add zero-trust rules: which request checks now happen at the gateway?
Add one more layer of defense in depth that has nothing to do with the network.
blocks.expected: Three zones with a gateway allowing only needed flows; gateway checks identity, device health, and authorization per request; an extra layer could be disk encryption on the file server or an offline backup, independent of the network.

cheatsheet: Defense in depth: stack layers so one failure is survivable.
Zero trust: verify explicitly, least privilege, assume breach; identity replaces network location.
Microsegmentation limits lateral movement; implicit deny is the default posture.
Secure-by-design: security is a requirement from day one, with threat modeling and safe defaults.
Shared responsibility: the provider secures the platform; the customer keeps data, identity, and access decisions.

checkpoint.prompt: A company allows any device on the office network to reach any internal server after one login at the VPN. Which architecture change best reflects zero trust?

choices.B: Require longer passwords at the VPN
choices.C: Move all servers to one stronger subnet
choices.D: Evaluate identity and device health for every request, with microsegmented access

checkpoint.explanation: Zero trust verifies each request explicitly and limits reach through least privilege and segmentation. Stronger perimeters or passwords keep the old trusted-inside assumption.
